claims.text: Structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles at high temperature is governed by selective formation of a self-passivating oxide layer.
Chromium in an alloy can form a compact, self-healing Cr2O3 layer that impedes further oxidation.
High configurational entropy slows atomic diffusion in near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
A protective oxide layer combined with high configurational entropy suppresses nanoparticle sintering and phase separation.
The initial nanoparticles are chemically homogeneous solid solutions without a preformed oxide layer.
Adding approximately 5 atom% Cr will provide a component that preferentially oxidizes to form a protective oxide.
The proposed test covers catalytic temperatures of 773–1173 K and thermoelectric temperatures of 473–1923 K in an oxidizing or reactive environment.
Cr doping will produce an in situ, uniform, self-healing Cr2O3 shell on the nanoparticle surface.
The reactive dopant oxidizes preferentially at high temperature.
The resulting oxide acts as a diffusion barrier and reduces further oxidation.
The oxide barrier reduces atomic diffusion responsible for nanoparticle coarsening and internal phase separation.
Cr-doped nanoparticles will retain particle size and phase homogeneity better than undoped nanoparticles during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Undoped nanoparticles will undergo more coarsening, phase separation, or compositional degradation than the Cr-doped nanoparticles under identical conditions.
The mechanism requires sufficient oxygen activity and temperatures at which a protective oxide is thermodynamically stable.
The mechanism may fail when the composition or environment prevents formation or preservation of the protective oxide.
The minimum Cr concentration and oxide-formation kinetics needed for effective passivation are not established.
Failure of Cr-doped particles to form a more protective oxide and to reduce degradation relative to the undoped control would falsify the proposed selective-oxide mechanism.
